Chemical technicians support research and development and quality control through laboratory testing, samples and instruments, and data records. O*NET lists 16 tasks: 12 core and 4 supplemental; core tasks include standard or experimental formulas, analysis and interpretation, sampling plans, training and safety audits, while supplemental tasks include pilot operations, directing production workers, designing experimental apparatus and developing new processes. Importance scores are not respondent percentages; development and signing authority must be checked separately for each position.

Signals to keep exploring: you can maintain precise laboratory operations and recordkeeping over long periods and are willing to take responsibility for the method, conditions and results of every test. O*NET work context shows that 100% of respondents in this occupation wear common protective or safety equipment daily, 100% use email daily, 99% have face-to-face discussions daily, 98% work indoors in environmentally controlled conditions daily, 95% encounter contaminants daily, 88% consider being exact or accurate extremely important, 59% consider working with a team extremely important, 51% are exposed to hazardous conditions daily, 48% face time pressure daily, 48% make decisions daily, 42% are in constant contact with others and 31% in contact most of the time, 39% constantly use their hands to handle or control objects and tools, 63% stand for more than half their working time, 34% consider repeating the same tasks extremely important, 26% have a lot of freedom in making decisions, and 60% have some freedom in determining tasks and priorities; 15% have highly automated work and 45% moderately automated work; 86% have regular schedules. These figures indicate that much of the work involves testing, preparation, recording and checking according to methods, with real responsibility for safety and reliable data, managed through institutionalized methods, review and records.

Conditions for pausing major investment: you have not yet completed a supervised exercise covering the full cycle of "understand the testing method and standards → confirm the status of samples, reagents and instruments → perform the test according to the method → record raw data → check anomalies and retest or escalate → issue or hand over results"; or you are unwilling to record each step according to the method, retain raw records honestly when results differ from expectations, or tend to issue results first and fill in records later when you do not understand the method's applicability. Do not skip method and safety judgments just because you "enjoy experiments": monitoring product quality according to specifications and maintaining a safe working environment is one of this occupation's important tasks. If you would rather design and scale up processes or develop new methods, chemical engineers and chemists are adjacent roles with different requirements.

Preparation level: O*NET Job Zone Three, with SVP6.0 to below 7.0, describes occupational preparation; BLS lists a typical associate's degree or two years of postsecondary education and moderate-term on-the-job training, rather than uniform requirements for every position. United States: BLS gives typical education and on-the-job training but does not establish a uniform exemption from licensing for all states and operations. The certification page lists 34 credentials and their issuing bodies; five registered apprenticeship titles appear separately in the occupational summary. Certifications, apprenticeships, job training and statutory licenses must each be verified and cannot substitute for one another. Mainland China: the Law on the Safety of Hazardous Chemicals takes effect on 2026-05-01; Article 5 requires hazardous chemical entities to provide training, assessment and protection. Only positions with qualification requirements must obtain qualifications as required by law; it is incorrect to say everyone who handles chemicals must obtain the same certificate. Institutions issuing data with evidentiary effect to the public must check CMA or special qualifications according to their applicable scope; reports are signed by authorized signatories within their technical competence, rather than every technician needing personal CMA accreditation.

Methods and data are a shared foundation, but this occupation does more than follow established methods: O*NET includes experimental formulas, experimental apparatus and new process development. Compare adjacent occupations by their work focus, project responsibilities and position authority; do not infer a lack of development or signing authority from the title "technician".

The editors group O*NET tasks into three areas of work: chemical technicians' work can be divided into three connected but distinct areas. The first is laboratory testing and analysis: perform chemical and physical tests according to standards or validated methods, set up and conduct experiments using chromatography, spectroscopy, separation techniques and microscopes, and monitor product quality against standards according to specifications. The second is sample, solution and reagent preparation and instrument maintenance: collect and prepare samples, prepare standard solutions and reagents according to formulas, maintain, clean and sterilize instruments and equipment, and record instrument use and calibration status. The third is data, records, reports and collaboration: compile and interpret test results, write technical reports and charts, participate in safety audits and corrective actions, provide technical support for chemists and engineers, and clearly hand over anomalies and actions taken. All three areas rely on methods, raw data and traceable records; their distinction lies in the authority to make judgments and sign off.
Perform tests according to validated methods and determine whether results are within controlled limits

Read and confirm testing methods, standards and decision rules → check sample identification and condition and expiry dates of reagents and reference materials → confirm instrument status, calibration and applicable conditions → perform tests according to the method and record raw data → compare quality control samples and historical data to identify anomalies → retain records of anomalies and report promptly, then decide according to procedures whether to investigate, retest or escalate → compile results and explain applicable conditions and limitations
Prepare solutions, reagents and samples and maintain and calibrate instruments

Check sampling points, batches and sample storage conditions → prepare samples according to the method and record pretreatment steps → prepare standard solutions and reagents according to formulas and label preparation and expiry dates → use and clean or sterilize instruments and vessels according to procedures → record instrument use and calibration or verification status → handle and report nonconforming or abnormal samples according to procedures

Compile and interpret test results and write reports or charts explaining methods, conditions and limitations; do not substitute estimates for measurements or alter raw data to fit expectations. Editorial advice: promptly retain raw records of anomalies and report them according to actual procedures; investigations should first check methods, samples, instruments and quality control. Retesting/resampling may take place only when procedures permit and safety conditions and authorization are in place; repeated testing must not be used to select passing values or delay safety action.

Six editorial checkpoints: method applicability, sample/reagent/instrument status, whether anomalies require immediate reporting or emergency procedures, completeness of raw records, adequacy of quality control evidence, and the report's applicable scope. This page does not impose a uniform order for retesting and shutdown.
Judgment one: whether the method and decision rules apply

First confirm whether the testing method, standards and decision rules cover the current sample matrix and concentration range, then decide whether direct testing is possible; report cases outside the method's scope and request confirmation instead of producing data first.
Judgment two: whether sample, reagent and instrument status is reliable

Check sample identification and storage conditions, reagent and reference material expiry dates, and instrument calibration or verification status; if any step is outside requirements, resolve it before testing rather than issuing results with unresolved questions.
Judgment three: boundaries for anomaly reporting, investigation and retesting

Editorial advice: promptly retain raw records of anomalies and report them according to actual procedures; investigations should first check methods, samples, instruments and quality control. Retesting/resampling may take place only when procedures permit and safety conditions and authorization are in place; repeated testing must not be used to select passing values or delay safety action.
Judgment four: whether raw data are complete and traceable

Raw records should include method numbers, sample identification, time, instruments, reagent batch numbers, key parameters and observations; changes must leave an audit trail with reasons, rather than overwriting or rewriting raw data.
Judgment five: whether quality control and trends support the conclusion

The editors check quality control samples, parallel samples and trends; their rules must be checked for the specific method, and trends do not automatically override measurements. Retain and report anomaly records promptly; do not delay action while awaiting review or selecting passing values, and do not treat a single sample result as representative of an unverified whole.
Judgment six: whether the report clearly states applicable conditions and limitations

Reports should explain methods, sample conditions, detection limits and uncertainty or limitations, and anomalies and actions taken, allowing readers to judge the scope in which conclusions can be used instead of providing only a number.

Chemical technicians perform chemical and physical laboratory tests to assist scientists in qualitative and quantitative analyses of solid, liquid and gaseous materials for research and development of new products or processes, quality control, maintenance of environmental standards, and other experimental, theoretical or practical applications of chemistry and related sciences (official duties for O*NET-SOC 19-4031.00). In daily work, they perform chemical or physical laboratory tests to assist qualitative or quantitative analysis; maintain, clean or sterilize laboratory instruments or equipment; monitor product quality to ensure compliance with standards and specifications; set up and conduct experiments and tests using chromatography, spectroscopy, physical or chemical separation techniques and microscopy; prepare chemical solutions for products or processes according to standard formulas or devise experimental formulas; compile and interpret results of tests and analyses; participate in safety programs and committees or teams and maintain a safe working environment through laboratory or plant safety audits; provide technical support or assistance to chemists or engineers; develop and conduct sampling and analysis plans to maintain quality standards of raw materials, intermediates or products; train new employees on topics such as proper laboratory equipment operation; write technical reports or prepare charts to document experimental results; order and inventory materials to maintain supplies; operate experimental pilot plants and assist with experimental design; direct or supervise other workers producing chemical products; design or fabricate experimental apparatus to develop new products or processes; and develop new chemical engineering processes or production techniques. Responsibility boundaries: technicians are responsible for testing according to methods, sample, reagent and instrument status, authentic and complete raw data, anomaly reporting, and retesting or escalation according to procedures. However, method confirmation and signing off conclusions, process changes and release approval, and testing reports subject to qualification accreditation are determined by positions and institutions with the necessary authorization and qualifications; this page cannot establish that technical positions universally hold these powers.

O*NET-SOC 19-4031.00 (Chemical Technicians): Job Zone Three (medium preparation), SVP range 6.0 to below 7.0; interest code IRC; the official list contains 16 tasks (12 core + 4 supplemental), with core task importance ranging from 88 (performing chemical or physical laboratory tests to assist qualitative or quantitative analysis) to 68 (ordering and inventorying materials); typical entry education is an associate's degree or two years of postsecondary education, with moderate-term on-the-job training.

These two values are industry mean proxies, rather than occupational medians for chemical technicians, and cannot establish starting pay or personal income; this page does not publish occupational values or convert U.S. figures to renminbi.

O*NET details explicitly give the 2025 industry distribution: manufacturing 43%, professional, scientific and technical services 31%; the current industry subpage likewise shows 43/31, with other industries at 26% (including wholesale). Industry structure is not wages. BLS2025–2035 projects 60,000→63,000 people, 5% (table 1.2 gives exactly 4.9%), with 7,600 average annual openings. Industry wage medians for month 5 of 2025 are retained: wholesale 65,960, R&D 63,900, chemical manufacturing 63,040, education 59,750, and testing laboratories 49,050 U.S. dollars/year.

Entry requirements, training and authority for each position must be separately verified against its own page and company policies; this table does not establish statutory duties or qualification rules.

The table below compares roles and occupations adjacent to this occupation: chemical engineers, industrial engineers, materials engineers, aerospace engineering and operations technicians, industrial engineering technicians and chemists. The four columns address the same kinds of questions: what each direction does, its key differences from this occupation, and who is better suited to choose it.

Chemical engineers mainly handle processes, plants and engineering design at scale; technicians mainly support R&D and quality control through experimental testing and data and may also participate in pilot operations and new process development. Their tasks may overlap; authority must be checked for the project.

People willing to explore calculations and scale-up judgments are suited to chemical engineering; those willing to consistently produce reliable data according to methods are suited to this occupation.
Design processes and plants and produce scale-up assessments and process documentation; the main outputs are calculations and process design documents.
Chemical Engineers

Industrial engineers work on system processes, efficiency and resource allocation; this occupation works on laboratory methods, samples and data, evaluated by data reliability and compliance with specifications.
People who enjoy processes, efficiency and coordination are suited to industrial engineering; those who enjoy the details of methods and data are suited to this occupation.
Optimize processes, human-machine systems, scheduling and costs; the main outputs are process proposals and efficiency metrics.
Industrial Engineers

Materials engineers evaluate materials and develop manufacturing processes, material selection proposals and failure analyses; chemical technicians focus on chemical and physical testing and data and may also participate in R&D. Both may test materials; their main outputs and position responsibilities distinguish them.

People willing to study material properties and failure mechanisms are suited to materials engineering; those willing to perform materials and chemical tests and ensure data quality are suited to this occupation.
Study material properties, material selection and failures and provide materials proposals; the main outputs are materials data and proposals.
Materials Engineers

Aerospace engineering and operations technicians focus on aerospace equipment, systems and testing support; chemical technicians focus on materials experiments and chemical data. Airworthiness, confidentiality and other requirements must be checked for the specific position; occupational titles cannot determine which side has stronger requirements.

People hoping to focus on aviation and aerospace are suited to aerospace engineering and operations technician roles; those willing to work in diverse laboratory environments are suited to this occupation.
Perform testing, assembly, operation and maintenance in aviation and aerospace; the main outputs are test data and operational records.
Aerospace Engineering and Operations Technicians

Industrial engineering technicians focus on on-site processes, working time and efficiency measurement; this occupation focuses on laboratory methods and chemical and physical testing, with different tools and systems of standards.
People who enjoy on-site measurement and process improvement are suited to industrial engineering technician roles; those who enjoy laboratory methods and instruments are suited to this occupation.
Support measurement and analysis of working time, motion, scheduling and process improvement; the main outputs are measurement data and improvement proposals.
Industrial Engineering Technicians

Chemists focus more on chemical research, experimental planning and interpretation of knowledge; technicians focus on experimental execution, instruments and data and may also develop experimental formulas or participate in process development. Education and research responsibilities must be checked for the specific position.

People willing to independently design experiments and interpret conclusions are suited to chemist roles; those willing to perform and record high-quality work according to methods are suited to this occupation.
Lead experimental design, method development and interpretation of conclusions; the main outputs are research reports and conclusions.
Chemists

If you would rather design processes and plants and make scale-up judgments, compare chemical engineers and materials engineers further; if you would rather optimize processes and efficiency, compare industrial engineers and industrial engineering technicians; if you hope to focus on aviation and aerospace testing and operations, compare aerospace engineering and operations technicians; if you would rather develop methods and interpret conclusions, compare chemists. Entry requirements and responsibility structures differ from this occupation, and the testing and recordkeeping judgments on this page should not be confused with authority to develop methods or sign off conclusions.

paragraphs: Boundary: the following six risk cards summarize this occupation's tasks and work environment to explain "what you may encounter and how it can be controlled", without incidence rates or accident probabilities; verify the applicability of each measure against company rules and local regulations separately.

Direct answer: this occupation's pressures most in need of advance assessment come from three areas: erroneous conclusions caused by unreliable data and inapplicable methods, safety and health exposure from laboratory chemicals and instrument operations, and untraceable responsibility caused by incomplete records and handovers. O*NET work context shows 88% consider being exact or accurate extremely important, 95% encounter contaminants daily, 51% are exposed to hazardous conditions daily, 48% face time pressure daily and 34% consider repeating the same tasks extremely important.

O*NET covers U.S. tasks/surveys; Articles 5/127 of China's hazardous chemical law concern training, protection and entry into force, and Articles 2/5/8/9/12–16 of the inspection and testing supervision measures concern applicability, competence, signing and records; the U.S. laboratory standard 1910.1450 separately requires checking (a)/(b) coverage. The following are editorial control suggestions, rather than uniform operating authorization.
Laboratory testing and analysis positions, and sample, instrument and quality positions

Errors in data or conclusions may cause batch misjudgments and incorrect product release, affect third-party decisions in environmental monitoring or external testing, and require corrective actions such as reinspection and recalls.

Check methods, detection limits/uncertainty against actual samples and reporting requirements; editorial advice: promptly retain raw records of anomalies and report them according to actual procedures; investigations should first check methods, samples, instruments and quality control. Retesting/resampling may take place only when procedures permit and safety conditions and authorization are in place; repeated testing must not be used to select passing values or delay safety action.

Issuing conclusions despite a method exceeding the sample matrix or concentration range, instruments being outside controlled conditions, or individual results being used to represent an entire batch's quality.
Positions involving chemicals, instruments and sample pretreatment

Chemical contact, reagent leaks, glassware, pressure vessels and high-temperature equipment may cause burns, poisoning, cuts and other injuries; long-term contact with contaminants may also create chronic health risks.

First check actual chemicals, safety information, exposure assessments and job training, then select protection, ventilation, labeling and waste disposal according to applicable procedures. U.S. 1910.1450 covers only situations meeting the definition of laboratory use, rather than all production or pilot operations; (e)/(f) concern chemical hygiene plans and training, rather than a uniform eyewash/shower configuration checklist. Report and handle leaks according to on-site emergency duties; this page does not authorize entering a leak area yourself. Article 5 of China's hazardous chemical law concerns training/protection; when personal safety is directly endangered, stop work as provided by law or evacuate after taking possible emergency measures and promptly report, rather than waiting for additional approval.
Skipping protection to meet deadlines or working in unsuitable places; continuing to use reagents with unclear labels or past expiry; mixing waste or failing to dispose of it by category.

Incomplete raw records or changes without audit trails can make results untraceable and prevent substantiation in audits and disputes; external testing reports may not be accepted if qualification and authorization requirements are unmet.

Retain raw records promptly according to applicable management requirements and leave audit trails for changes; Article 2 of China's Measures for the Supervision and Administration of Inspection and Testing Institutions applies to activities issuing reports with evidentiary effect to the public; Articles 8 and 12 concern signatory competence and technical scope, and Article 13 requires raw records and reports to be kept for at least 6 years. values: Fictional sample package | Use only paper and pencil or spreadsheets, 100 minutes; no reagent preparation or instrument operation.

Samples A/B are fictional aqueous solutions; the problem's method T1 applies to diluted readings of 0–5 mg/L, with an original sample reference range of 20–30 mg/L; neither is a real-world standard. Original sample concentration = reading × dilution factor; relative difference between parallel results = absolute difference between the two values/mean × 100%, with the stipulated limit ≤5%; QC reference 2.00 mg/L, recovery = measured/reference × 100%, with the stipulated 90%–110%. If QC fails, the whole batch awaits verification, without a release judgment.

2026-10-03 records: A1/A2 readings 2.40/2.50 mg/L, each diluted 10-fold; QC reading 2.30 mg/L (undiluted); B1/B2 readings 2.10/2.12 mg/L, with only "10?" in the factor field and no preparation record. Raw data must not be deleted or changed.

Register: complete handovers for samples A/B, IDs A-03/B-03; QC reference material S01 valid until 2026-12-31, with recorded batch S01; instrument I01 calibration valid until 2026-09-30, and I02 valid until 2026-12-31 with its check passed that day. In this problem, I02 is permitted by method T1; do not substitute other instruments independently. Trainee operator P, reviewer R and approver Q each record their names.
Task | Calculations, judgment boundaries and handover.

Calculate A's two original sample concentrations, mean, relative difference between parallel results and QC recovery. State which values can be confirmed arithmetically and which quality conclusions cannot be reached; for B, first list evidence to obtain, without guessing the factor.

Mark I01 expiry and affected records and propose a plan for suspension, verification, escalation and approved retesting on I02; do not actually operate it. The handover must state samples/batches, original values, reference material batches, instruments, times, pending items and P/R/Q responsibilities.
Reference solution | Correct arithmetic does not equal valid data.

A = 24.0/25.0 mg/L, mean 24.5, relative difference between parallel results 1.0/24.5×100%=4.08%; only this item meets the stipulated ≤5%. QC = 2.30/2.00×100%=115%, exceeding 110%; A falling within 20–30 does not justify reporting it as passing. Both failed QC and expired I01 require suspending release of this batch's results and reporting to Q.

B's factor has no evidence, so its original sample concentration cannot be confirmed; if 10-fold dilution is calculated purely hypothetically, the values are 21.0/21.2, mean 21.1 and relative difference 0.95%, marked only as "hypothetical calculations", rather than entered as formal results. Require checking original preparation records and responsible personnel; if evidence is missing, repeat preparation and testing according to procedures.

Isolate and mark I01 status and retain original records; R checks QC preparation, reference material batches and instrument status, and Q confirms the affected scope and retesting plan. I02 has the stipulated applicability qualification and check records but still requires Q's approval and confirmation that QC is under control before retesting A/B; do not automatically reuse old values or independently extend calibration. Evaluate calculations, handling of both failure types and complete handover, rather than whether "pass" is written.
